analytic.title: Integration of Preemption Threshold and Quantum-Based Scheduling for Schedulability Enhancement of Fixed Priority Tasks

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Fixed priority scheduling is an important real-time scheduling scheme widely used in practice. To improve the schedulability of fixed priority scheduling considerable effort has been made such as introduction of preemption threshold or deferred preemption, and quantum-based scheduling. In this paper, we develop a new scheduling scheme by introducing both preemption threshold and quantum into one scheduling framework. The new scheduling method may successfully schedule tasks which are not schedulable either by preemption threshold scheduling or quantum-based scheduling, as well as tasks schedulable by either scheduling, thus improves the schedulability of fixed-priority tasks. We analyze the schedulability of the new scheduler by computing the worst case response time of tasks. Based on the analysis, we developed an algorithm for assignment of preemption threshold and quantum sizes.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Fixed priority scheduling such as the Rate Monotonic (RM) algorithm [1] or the Deadline Monotonic (DM) algorithm [2] has been widely used in real-time systems because it is efficient to implement [3], though the Earliest Deadline First (EDF) algorithm can achieve higher processor utilization theoretically for both preemptive [1] and non-preemptive [4] real-time scheduling on a uniprocessor. There has been much research to improve the schedulability of fixed priority tasks including works in [5], [6], [7]. In general, preemptive schedulers give better schedulability than non-preemptive schedulers. However, it has been shown that in the context of fixed priority scheduling, preemptive schedulers are not always superior to non-preemptive schedulers in [7], [8].

Preemption threshold scheduling [7] is a dual priority scheduling scheme that improves schedulability of fixed priority tasks. While the priority of a task is used to preempt other tasks, Preemption threshold is the effective priority when a task is running. Both preemptive and nonpreemptive scheduling are special cases of scheduling with preemption threshold [7]. When each task's preemption threshold is equal to its priority, then we have preemptive scheduling. If each task has its priority equal to the highest priority among tasks, then we have non-preemptive scheduling.

Another approach to enhance the schedulability in fixed priority scheduling is quantum-based scheduling. Under quantum-based scheduling, processor time is allocated to tasks in discrete time units called quantum. Quantumbased scheduling can be defined as follows [9]: when a processor is allocated to some task, that task is guaranteed to execute without preemption for quantum time units, or until it terminates, whichever comes first. Quantum-based scheduling is similar to preemption threshold scheduling in the sense that both provide a continuum of scheduling spaces. Non-preemptive and preemptive scheduling can be viewed as the extreme endpoints in a continuum of quantum-based scheduling: a non-preemptive system results when the quantum size of each task is infinite, and a fully preemptive system results when the quantum size of each task is zero.

Recently, it was shown that there is a task set which is schedulable by quantum-based scheduling, but not schedulable by preemption threshold scheduling [10]. However, quantum-based scheduling is not always superior to preemption threshold scheduling, so there is also a task set which is not schedulable by quantum-based scheduling but schedulable by preemption threshold scheduling. In this paper, we present a new scheduling scheme that integrates quantum-based scheduling and preemption threshold. The integrated scheduler can successfully schedule task sets that are schedulable either by preemption threshold scheduling or by quantum-based scheduling. We analyze the schedulability of quantum-based scheduling with preemption threshold by developing a computation method for the worst case response time. And we present an algorithm for assignment of preemption threshold and quantum size based on the previous research results.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. We briefly review related work in Section 2. Section 3 explains the system model, assumptions, and definitions. Section 4 provides examples of quantum-based scheduling and preemption threshold scheduling. The examples show that some task sets can be successfully scheduled by quantumbased scheduling but not by preemption threshold scheduling, and preemption threshold scheduling is superior to quantum-based scheduling for some task sets. And we present a new scheduling method by introducing preemption threshold to quantum-based scheduling. Section 5 analyzes the worst case response time of tasks when they are scheduled by quantum-based preemption threshold scheduling. In Section 6, we present an algorithm to assign preemption threshold and quantum sizes when priorities of tasks are predefined. Finally we conclude our work in Section 7.

div.head: Related Work
div.p: With fixed priority preemptive scheduling, Deadline Monotonic (DM) scheduling is shown to be optimal [2]. As a special case of DM scheduling, Rate Monotonic (RM) scheduling is optimal when the relative deadline of tasks is equal to the period [1]. However, it was shown in [8] that DM is no longer optimal in the context of non-preemptive fixed priority scheduling. In [8], the schedulability of nonpreemptive fixed priority scheduling is analyzed using the concept of level-i busy period introduced by Lehoczky [11]. The concept of level-i busy period plays an important role in analyzing both the schedulability of preemption threshold scheduling [7] and quantum-based scheduling [10]. Schedulability analysis of fixed priority scheduling is based on the analysis of the worst case response time in level-i busy period introduced in [12].

Wang and Saksena showed preemption threshold scheduling can improve the schedulablity of fixed priority tasks [7]. Regehr [13] made a correction in the response time analysis of Wang and Saksena, and extended its application. In [14], it is shown that multiple valid preemption threshold assignments form a solution space, which provides useful scheduling options. Further studies of preemption threshold scheduling can be found in [15], [16], and the application of the preemption threshold to dynamic priority scheduling is discussed in [17].

In [5], they studied both preemption threshold scheduling and quantum-based scheduling (called delayed preemption in their work), and reported empirical results that show quantum-based scheduling can increase processor utilization with RM priority assignment [5]. The worst case response time of the fixed-priority scheduling with delayed (deferred) preemption is analyzed in [18]. For fixed priority scheduling, previous work in [19] analyzed the disadvantages of the quantum for schedulability: a blocking time introduced by the non-preemptive region, due to quantumbased scheduling. In [10], the schedulablity of quantumbased scheduling when all tasks have the same quantum size is analyzed. Quantum-based scheduling was applied to dynamic priority scheduling for efficient object sharing [9], flow protection in communication [20], and reduction of the scheduling overhead [21].

div.head: System Model and Definitions
div.p: A periodic task is denoted by τ i , and a periodic task set is represented by the collection of periodic tasks, τ = {τ i }. Each τ i has (T i , D i , C i ) where T i is the period, D i is the relative deadline, and C i is the worst case execution time. In this paper, we assume that T i ≥ D i ≥ C i > 0. Time is discrete and clock ticks are indexed by integers, as in [4]. Tasks are all independent and cannot be suspended by themselves.

Each τ i is assigned a priority π i . When π i is higher than π j , it is denoted as π i ≺ π j . For a given task τ i , we define hp(τ i ) = {τ j |π j ≺ π i }, and lp(τ i ) = {τ j |π i ≺ π j }. The worst case response time (WCRT) of τ i is defined as the maximum possible response time among all instances of τ i . We will denote the WCRT of τ i as W CRT i .

Preemption threshold scheduling assigns a value called preemption threshold to each task. The preemption threshold of a task τ i is denoted as γ i , which must be a priority value higher than or equal to π i . When a task τ i is released, it competes for the processor at priority π i . After τ i starts its execution, another task τ j can preempt τ i if and only if π j ≺ γ i . If γ i = π i , scheduling of τ i is equivalent to preemptive scheduling. If γ i is equal to the highest priority, it is equivalent to non-preemptive scheduling.

A quantum is a task variable, which is a unit of non-preemptive execution. The quantum of a task τ i is denoted as q i . When a task τ i is scheduled, τ i can execute during q i without being preempted by other tasks, unless it finishes its execution before the quantum expires. Thus, τ i is non-preemptive for q i time units. If the task finishes before the quantum expires, another task is selected to execute. If τ i does not finish after execution of q i units, it can be preempted by any ready task in hp(τ i ). If the quantum size q i = 0, quantum-based scheduling of τ i is equivalent to preemptive scheduling. On the other hand, if q i = C i , scheduling of τ i is equivalent to non-preemptive scheduling.

div.head: Preemption Threshold Scheduling vs. Quantum-Based Scheduling
div.p: We present examples of the two scheduling schemes to see their behaviors. Consider an example task set from [7].
div.formula: γ 3 = π 2 . If we let γ 3 = π 1 , W CRT 1 is 59 (> 50).
div.p: Thus this task set is not schedulable by preemption threshold scheduling, as shown in [10].

By choosing an appropriate quantum size, we can make the modified tasks schedulable. In this case, there are many possible values of the quantum size. As an example we choose 20 as the quantum size for all tasks (q i = 20). Figure 1 shows the worst case response time of τ 3 in RM priority ordering when q i = 20.
The higher priority tasks τ 1 and τ 2 are simultaneously released with τ 3 . At time 25, the time quantum of τ 1

has not yet expired, but since τ 1 has finished its job, τ 2 is scheduled. At time 65, τ 3 exceeds the bounds of its quantum, but since there is no other task to execute, τ 3 is allowed to continue its execution. Though τ 1 is released again at time 70, since the time quantum of τ 3 has not yet expired, τ 3 completes its execution, to time 80. With q i = 20, the worst case response times of tasks are: 44, 64, and 80 for τ 1 , τ 2 , and τ 3 respectively (the calculation of the worst case response time will be discussed in the next section). Therefore, this task set is schedulable by quantum-based scheduling.

However, quantum-based scheduling is not superior to preemption threshold scheduling in terms of schedulability. Let us add a task τ 0 = (50, 1, 1) to the original task set. Then the task set becomes: {(50, 1, 1), (70, 50, 20), (80, 80, 20), (200, 100, 35)}. Apparently, the only possible quantum size is 1, because if any q i is greater than 1, τ 0 could miss the deadline. When the quantum size is equal to 1, the scheduling is equivalent to fully preemptive scheduling. As shown in [7], this task set is not schedulable by preemptive RM. Thus this task set is not schedulable by quantumbased scheduling. However, this task set is schedulable by preemption threshold scheduling as shown in Figure 2. In this example, π 0 ≺ π 1 ≺ π 2 ≺ π 3 and γ 0 = π 0 , γ 1 = π 1 , γ 2 = π 1 , and γ 3 = π 2 .

div.head: Integration of Quantum-Based Scheduling and Preemption Threshold
div.p: Inspecting the above examples, we can see that the task set {τ 0 = (50, 1, 1), τ 1 = (70, 50, 25), τ 2 = (80, 80, 20), τ 3 = (200, 100, 35)}, which is obtained by adding τ 0 to the example task set of [7] and changing C 1 to 25, is not schedulable either by preemption threshold scheduling or quantum-based scheduling. To make this task set schedulable, we integrate the two scheduling schemes in the following way:
1) If π i ≺ γ j , τ i can preempt the running task τ j .
2) If π i ≺ π j but γ j π i , τ i cannot preempt the running task τ j before q j is expired.

3) When the quantum of τ j is expired, tasks with π i ≺ π j can preempt τ j . Rule 1 is adopted from preemption threshold scheduling, Rule 2 integrates quantum-based scheduling with preemption threshold, and Rule 3 is from quantum-based scheduling. Note that the running task's priority is not changed to its preemption threshold. This is different from the original preemption threshold scheduling, in which the priority of the running task is set to its preemption threshold value.

Figure 3 shows the integrated scheduler successfully schedule the above task set using the settings in Table 1 (the smaller the number, the higher the priority). Table 1 also shows the worst case response times of tasks.

Apparently, if γ i is equal to the highest priority for all τ i , integrated scheduling is equivalent to quantum-based scheduling. On the other hand, if q i = C i for all τ i , it is equivalent to preemption threshold scheduling, because any task with γ j π i cannot preempt the running task τ j during τ j 's execution by Rule 2. Therefore, the new integrated scheduler can successfully schedule task sets that are schedulable by preemption threshold scheduling or quantum-based scheduling.

div.head: Preemption Threshold and Quantum Size Assignment
div.p: Even though priorities are predefined for a task set, solution space for valid preemption threshold assignments or quantum sizes that make the task set schedulable might be very large [10], [14]. The solution space for quantumbased scheduling with preemption threshold could be even larger, because we need to consider both quantum sizes and preemption thresholds. In this section, we present a method to assign preemption threshold values and quantum sizes by limiting the search space.

Since it is difficult to assign preemption threshold and quantum size to a task simultaneously, we can try to assign one value first and then the other value later. For example, we can assign preemption threshold values using the research results of [7], [14] first, and when we cannot find a valid preemption threshold assignment we can try to assign quantum sizes. But the algorithm for preemption threshold in [7], [14] cannot be directly applied to the integrated scheduling, because any change in quantum size of lower priority tasks may affect the worst case respone time of higher priority tasks. To develop an algorithm for preemption threshold and quantum size assignment, let us analyze the properties of the quantum-based scheduling with preemption threshold.
Firstly, it is trivial that the worst case response time of a task τ i is not affected by tasks with preemption threshold lower than π i because of Rule 1.
Lemma 1: W CRT i is not affected by any task τ j such that π i ≺ γ j .

Secondly, as in preemption threshold scheduling, when there are multiple preemption threshold values that can make a task schedulable, we can assign the lowest preemption threshold among them to the task.

Theorem 2: Assume that a task set τ = {τ i } is schedulable with a set of {π i , γ i , q i }. If a task τ i is schedulable with assignment {π i , γ i , q i } where γ i ≺ γ i , then the task set is also schedulable by changing τ i 's preemption threshold to γ i .

Proof: By Lemma 1, lowering the preemption threshold of τ i does not affect the worst case execution time of tasks with priority higher than γ i . Also, a task τ j with priority γ i π j ≺ γ i will have no worse W CRT j with γ i than with γ i because the interference and the blocking time during their execution are decreased. When τ j has priority γ i π j ≺ π i , the worst case response time remains the same. Lemma 2: Assume that a task τ i is not schedulable with preemption threshold γ i and q i = C i . If B i is the minimum possible value, τ i is not schedulable with any quantum size with preemption threshold value γ i .

Proof: From Rule 2 and Rule 3, we can see that the interference due to higher priority tasks is minimized when q i = C i for a given preemption threshold. If we change q i to a value smaller than C i , higher priority tasks can preempt τ i during execution by Rule 3. Since B i is the minimum possible value, we cannot reduce the blocking time by decreasing the quantum size of a lower priority task. Therefore, if τ i is not schedulable with q i = C i , it is not schedulable with a given preemption threshold.

The difference from the algorithm for preemption threshold assignment described in [7] is that lines 1, 2, 3, and 12 are added. The first three lines initialize the quantum sizes as C i . Since each task is assigned the smallest quantum size at line 12, by Lemma 2, if we cannot find a valid preemption threshold for a task with q i = C i , the task is not schedulable. div.head: Conclusion
div.p: In this paper, we present a new scheduling method for fixed priority real-time tasks that utilizes both the concept of quantum and preemption threshold. It is shown that either quantum-based scheduling or preemption threshold scheduling is always superior to the other in terms of schedulablity. We developed rules to introduce both concepts into a scheduling framework, so any task set that can be scheduled either by preemption threshold scheduling or quantum-based scheduling is successfully scheduled. By providing more options in scheduling, task sets that are not schedulable either by two scheduling schemes can be made to be schedulable. Also, we compute the worst case response time of tasks under the new scheduling method based on previous studies of preemption threshold scheduling and quantum-based scheduling. An algorithm for preemption threshold and quantum size assignment is developed for the proposed scheduling method. Based on the analysis of the properties of quantum-based scheduling with preemption threshold, the algorithm finds a valid assignment set of preemption threshold and quantum sizes if one exists.
